At 4:17 in the morning, the city belongs to the things that cannot sleep.

The traffic lights continue changing for no one. Red, green, yellow. Their colors spill onto the wet streets and vanish beneath tires, though there are fewer tires now, fewer reasons to go anywhere. A cat sits beneath the awning of a closed bakery, watching the rain gather in the gutters. Somewhere, a refrigerator hums behind a wall. Somewhere else, a woman turns over in bed and dreams she is late.

The city is full of small, private emergencies.

On the seventh floor of an apartment building with cracked windows and a tired elevator, a man named Elias sits at his kitchen table. He has been sitting there for three hours. Before him is a cup of coffee that has gone cold, a chipped bowl containing two oranges, and a letter he has not opened.

The letter arrived yesterday.

It is white, except where the rain darkened the lower corner. His name is written across the front in handwriting he recognizes immediately. That is the difficulty. If the handwriting belonged to a stranger, he could tear the envelope in half and throw it away. If it belonged to someone he hated, he could burn it. But the handwriting belongs to his mother, and his mother has been dead for six years.

Elias lifts the envelope.

The apartment remains silent.

He turns it over. There is no return address.

He tells himself this is a mistake. A prank. Some administrative confusion. A letter forwarded from an old address by someone who does not know what happened. There are explanations, each one ordinary enough to be believed.

Still, the handwriting.

He places the envelope back on the table.

Outside, the rain begins to thin.

Across the street, in the dark window of a tailor’s shop, Elias sees his own reflection. He looks older than he expected. Not old, exactly. Just postponed. His face has the strained expression of a person who has been waiting for instructions.

He remembers his mother’s kitchen: the blue curtains, the chipped yellow kettle, the radio that only worked if you struck it twice on the side. She used to sing while washing dishes, but she never sang the whole song. Only the first line, repeated until it became something else. A promise without an ending.

When he was ten, he asked her why she never finished.

“Because,” she said, “the ending is where things stop.”

At the time, he thought this was wisdom. Later, he decided it was fear.

Now he is not sure there is a difference.

At 4:32, someone knocks on his door.

Elias does not move.

The knock comes again. Not loud. Not impatient. Three measured taps, the way his mother used to knock when he was a teenager and pretending not to be home.

His chair scrapes the floor.

The hallway outside is unlit. The bulb has been dead for months, and the landlord keeps promising to replace it. Elias stands behind the door and listens. He hears the building settling: pipes contracting, wooden beams sighing, the distant cough of a neighbor. Then, beneath these familiar sounds, he hears breathing.

“Who is it?” he asks.

No answer.

He looks through the peephole.

The hallway is empty.

He opens the door.

On the mat sits a small cardboard box tied with red string. There is no name on it. No label. The string is damp.

Elias brings it inside and places it beside the letter.

He does not open either.

The morning arrives without announcing itself. The rain stops. Pale light enters the kitchen and reveals the dust on every surface. The city begins again: buses groaning, doors slamming, voices rising through walls.

Elias makes fresh coffee.

At 7:10, his phone rings. It is his sister, Mara.

“Are you awake?” she asks.

“Yes.”

There is a pause. “Did you get something?”

Elias looks at the envelope and the box.

“How did you know?”

“I got one too.”

The silence between them is large enough to contain childhood.

“What does yours say?” he asks.

“I haven’t opened it.”

“Where is it?”

“With me.”

“Are you all right?”

Mara laughs once, without humor. “I don’t know. Are you?”

He looks toward the window. The tailor’s shop is open now. A man in a white shirt stands inside, arranging spools of thread by color. Red beside red. Blue beside blue. The careful order of things.

“I’m fine,” Elias says.

“You always say that.”

“So do you.”

Another pause.

Then Mara says, “Do you remember the night she disappeared?”

Elias closes his eyes.

Their mother had not died in a hospital. She had died in her sleep, quietly, without drama. But years before that, when they were children, she had disappeared for one night. She had left after dinner and returned just before dawn, carrying a paper bag and smelling of cold air.

They had asked where she went.

“Nowhere,” she said.

Their father accepted this answer. Elias did not. He remembered the fear of that night, the two children sitting on the stairs, listening for the key in the lock. He remembered deciding that love was the name for waiting beside a door.

“What about it?” he asks.

“I found the box,” Mara says. “It was in the storage room. Behind the old heater.”

Elias looks at the box on his table.

“Mine came this morning.”

“Maybe we should open them together.”

“When?”

“Now.”

They remain on the phone.

Elias takes the red string between his fingers. It is tied in a simple bow. He pulls.

Inside the box is a photograph.

It shows two children standing beside a river, their faces turned away from the camera. Elias recognizes the coats they wore. He recognizes the crooked fence. He recognizes the small white house in the distance.

But he does not remember the photograph.

On the back, in his mother’s handwriting, are six words:

You were there. You both saw.

Elias’s phone is still pressed to his ear.

“What did you get?” he asks.

Mara’s voice has changed. It sounds younger.

“A key,” she says.

“To what?”

“I don’t know.”

Beyond the window, the traffic lights keep changing. Red, green, yellow. The city moves through its rituals, carrying its secrets from one hour to the next.

Elias touches the photograph.

For the first time in six years, he remembers the river.

He remembers his mother kneeling in the grass.

He remembers another woman standing beside her.

And he remembers that the woman was crying.

Then, from somewhere deep within the apartment building, a door opens.

Someone begins walking up the stairs.
